rationale: Tests understanding of Bowman's layer regeneration — a classic OP exam trap; students often confuse it with epithelium which does regenerate.
Corneal transparency maintenance is a high-yield topic; the primary pump mechanism (Na-K-ATPase endothelial pump) is often confused with the avascular nature or the lamellar arrangement.
Differentiating buphthalmos from megalocornea is a classic OP clinical trap tested in exams; the IOP and Haab's striae are the key discriminators.
Interstitial keratitis from congenital syphilis is associated with Hutchinson's triad — a classic association that differentiates it from other causes.
Organism-to-drug matching in keratitis is the highest-yield OP trap; students confuse natamycin (fungal) with acyclovir (HSV) and voriconazole vs natamycin for filamentous vs yeast.
Acanthamoeba keratitis in contact lens wearers is another high-yield trap — the pathognomonic ring infiltrate and PHMB treatment are commonly tested.
Students often confuse nebula/macula/leucoma grading — the distinguishing feature is visibility through the opacity, not size.
Choosing the correct keratoplasty type for a given opacity is a practical application question that requires understanding both anatomy and procedure selection.
Schirmer's test interpretation and TBUT cutoffs are frequently tested clinical data points that students confuse — especially Schirmer I vs II and normal vs abnormal cutoffs.
Cyclosporine A (0.05–0.1%) eye drops are an immunomodulatory treatment for moderate-severe dry eye — not an artificial tear substitute, a trap students fall into.
Bitot's spots and the stages of xerophthalmia (X1A→X3B→XN) are high-yield for OP and preventive medicine exams — students confuse the staging.
Trachoma epidemiology — SAFE strategy and Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes — is an important public health topic tested in OP.
Graft rejection signs — especially the Khodadoust line (endothelial rejection line) — are a high-yield clinical trap. Students often misidentify the type of rejection.
DSEK/DSAEK vs DMEK is a contemporary distinction — DMEK gives faster visual recovery but has a higher rebubbling rate, which is a common exam question.
The preservation medium and maximum storage time for corneas are high-yield — students confuse moist chamber (4°C, 48h) with organ culture (4°C/37°C, 28 days).
Contraindications to eye donation are commonly tested — especially distinguishing absolute contraindications (rabies, CJD, unknown cause of death) from relative ones.
Rust ring management after metallic FB removal is a practical OP clinical question — the timing of rust ring removal (immediate vs delayed) is a common trap.
The Seidel test is the key bedside test for wound leak after FB removal or any anterior segment procedure — commonly asked in OSCE stations.
